item.title: Indian space startup SatSure raises ₹60 crore from govt-backed space fund
item.description: The investment is part of a ₹200 crore Series B round that includes fresh equity, venture debt and secondary transactions, which the Bengaluru-based startup expects to close by December 2026 ...
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Indian space startup SatSure has raised ₹60 crore ($7 million) from a government-backed space technology fund as part of an ongoing ₹200 crore funding round, the company said on Friday.The investment comes as India seeks to expand its commercial space industry through reforms that have opened the traditionally state-dominated sector to private companies and investors.The Antariksh Venture Capital Fund is investing at a post-money valuation of ₹870 crore ($93 million), SatSure said. The ₹1,600 crore fund is anchored by IN-SPACe, India's private space sector regulator, and managed by SIDBI Venture Capital, an arm of state-owned small-business lender SIDBI.Bengaluru-based SatSure uses satellite imagery and artificial intelligence to help banks, insurers, infrastructure firms and government agencies make decisions. Its subsidiary KaleidEO develops satellite imaging systems for Earth observation.The series B round comprises ₹165 crore in fresh equity, ₹25 crore in venture debt and ₹10 crore in secondary transactions. The company expects to close the round by December 2026.The proceeds will help prepare its satellite imaging payloads for launch in 2027, support its participation in India's planned Earth-observation satellite network and expand its data analysis capabilities and international operations.SatSure's customers include HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, Axis Bank, ITC, Bayer and the Airports Authority of India.The startup has raised ₹427 crore from institutional investors, excluding grants, with previous backers including Baring Private Equity Partners India, Promus Ventures and Asian Development Bank Ventures.

Home / Industry / Agriculture / India's wheat acreage may see steepest fall in 26 years on water shortage

India's wheat acreage may see steepest fall in 26 years on water shortage Weak monsoon rains have prompted farmers in key growing states to shift to less water-intensive crops such as chickpeas, raising concerns over wheat output and food inflation

India's main winter-sown crop, wheat usually competes for acreage with rapeseed, chickpeas and corn (Photo: PTI)

Reuters JALNA 3 min read Last Updated : Nov 20 2026 | 12:14 PM IST

Listen to This Article

India's wheat acreage is poised for its steepest decline in 26 years as fields parched by the weakest monsoon rains in more than a decade spur farmers to switch to competing crops in search of better returns, industry officials told Reuters. The drop in planting, coupled with the risk of lower yields brought by a severe El Niño weather pattern, threatens to curb output in the world's second-largest wheat producer, in turn boosting prices and complicating efforts to damp food inflation. "Wheat needs to be irrigated at least four to five times, but we don't have enough water even to sow the crop," said farmer Vilas Bhutekar in the Jalna district of the western state of Maharashtra.   "So we chose chickpeas instead, as they require less water." India's main winter-sown crop, wheat usually competes for acreage with rapeseed, chickpeas and corn. Also Read

PM-Kisan 24th instalment: PM Modi to release ₹18,680 crore on October 30

Wheat acreage likely to remain steady despite weak monsoon rainfall

India's June-September monsoon rains were the lowest in more than a decade as the drying effect of the El Niño drove rainfall as much as 41 per cent below average in key wheat-growing states such as Punjab, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra. "Wheat needs more water than other competing crops," said Nitin Gupta, deputy country head at agricultural trader Olam Agri India. "But water is in short supply in some regions this year, which could mean farmers plant less wheat." Wheat was planted across 5 million hectares (12 million acres) by Nov. 13, down 15.3 per cent from a year earlier, government data show. Planting for the 2026/27 season is expected to fall about 6 per cent from last year's record of 33.6 million hectares (83 million acres), an average estimate by 10 industry officials shows. That would be the steepest decline since 2000/01, taking area under the crop to the lowest in four years at 31.58 million hectares (78 million acres). Crop shift Wheat acreage is expected to stay largely steady in the key northern states of Haryana and Punjab, which have access to reliable irrigation. But farmers in other states are likely to shift from wheat to less-thirsty crops such as chickpea and rapeseed, industry officials said. Prices of these crops have risen much more than wheat, prompting farmers to shift acreage away from the grain, said Sandeep Bansal, director of a flour miller based in the northern state of Uttar Pradesh. "Wheat is usually farmers' first choice, but this year other crops are giving better returns," Bansal said. The state-run Food Corporation of India buys wheat from farmers at the minimum support price, which New Delhi raised this year by just 1 per cent to 2,610 rupees per 100 kg, the smallest increase since 2002/03. "The government typically incentivises wheat planting by raising procurement prices by 5 to 6 per cent annually," said a New Delhi-based trader with a global trade house. "This year's 1 per cent hike is, in fact, discouraging farmers from expanding wheat acreage."

item.description: Annmarie Hordern was denied access to Thursday's trilateral meeting in Shenzhen after asking Trump whether former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had been disloyal to the US ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / China bars Bloomberg reporter from Trump-Xi meet after question on Nvidia

China bars Bloomberg reporter from Trump-Xi meet after question on Nvidia Annmarie Hordern was denied access to Thursday's trilateral meeting in Shenzhen after asking Trump whether former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had been disloyal to the US

Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump arrive for a trilateral meeting at Kylin Villa on November 19, 2026 in Shenzhen, China | Win McNamee/Pool via REUTERS

AP New York 3 min read Last Updated : Nov 20 2026 | 8:26 AM IST

Listen to This Article

It's a scenario seen every day: A reporter shouts a question out to a leader at an event. The leader either answers or ignores it. In China, though, Bloomberg TV journalist Annmarie Hordern was blocked from a key event by Chinese officials, apparently as retribution for having shouted a question in a way that the government considered rude. Hordern was barred from Thursday's trilateral meeting among President Donald Trump, Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China, after having called out a question during a Trump meeting with Xi. She had asked Trump if former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had been disloyal to the United States.

A White House official said the Chinese insisted the reporter not be allowed in despite the White House having pushed for admission. The official insisted on speaking on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity around the issue. The White House did not immediately respond to a query about what steps it took to advocate for the reporter. Jacqui Heinrich, president of the White House Correspondents' Association, said on X that it was "commendable that the WH is advocating for press access". A pool report from the incident said the Chinese "have passed along a message that yelling questions is considered extremely rude and we will be pulled from the room if we do so".

Also Read

Time-limited, auctioned export quotas beat blanket trade restrictions

India must turn China trade dependence into domestic value addition premium

China's Foreign Ministry did not respond to a request for comment from The Associated Press, and an email to Bloomberg seeking comment was not immediately returned. The incident, which reflected the way China typically seeks to tightly control news events, recalled a previous one in 2022, in which a White House pool reporter said she was knocked off balance after being yanked by her backpack when she tried to shout a question to President Joe Biden. The question was about human rights ahead of a meeting between Biden and Xi in Bali, Indonesia. The reporter lost balance without falling and was pushed towards the door, a pool report said at the time. Two White House staff members intervened and said the producer should be left alone.

China's approach to journalists, particularly foreign media, has long been chilly and uneven. In recent decades, international reporters have been expelled both for their coverage and for perceived misbehavior during news events. Resident correspondents are occasionally detained and questioned -- and in some cases in past years, compelled to sign "self-criticism" reports -- for showing up where the government doesn't want them to be. Chinese journalists who stray from the party line can face even more stringent measures, including censorship, dismissal and at times even imprisonment.

item.title: How India taxes foreign investors' share gains and how peers compare
item.description: India charges foreign portfolio investors the same capital gains tax as residents, while several large markets exempt them; the government is now examining the issue ...
item.dc:creator: Vedant Vichare
item.content:encoded: The finance ministry is examining calls to scrap the long-term capital gains (LTCG) tax on foreign portfolio investors (FPIs), but any decision will come only in the Budget, Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) chairman Ravi Agrawal said on November 16. The Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) has reportedly recommended the move, Reuters reported on November 2. The recommendation is not binding, and the Union Budget is due in February 2027. What India charges foreign investors India taxes FPIs on listed equities at the same rates as residents. Gains on shares held for more than 12 months are taxed at 12.5 per cent above Rs 1.25 lakh a year, and gains on shares held for up to 12 months at 20 per cent. Foreign investors also pay securities transaction tax (STT) of 0.1 per cent on both the purchase and the sale of shares taken for delivery, whether or not they make a profit.  China exempts foreign investors from corporate income tax on gains from shares of mainland Chinese companies, known as A-shares, according to PwC’s analysis of two notices issued jointly by its finance ministry, tax administration and securities regulator in November 2014. Foreigners mainly reach these shares through Stock Connect, a trading link with Hong Kong, or as licensed institutional investors (QFII or RQFII) with no business presence in China. The exemption applies to gains from November 17, 2014, and earlier gains remain taxable. Such gains are otherwise taxed at 10 per cent, and the exemption is temporary in name: it rests on an administrative circular, not a law, and has been in place for more than 10 years, KPMG Luxembourg noted in March 2026.What the government has said Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said on November 2 that the government would consider the representations it has received on the capital gains tax structure, and that India needs capital to sustain growth. Agrawal said on November 16 that points raised by stakeholders were being examined and that “Any decision would be taken only in the Budget”. The case for relief Saurabh Mukherjea, founder and chief investment officer of Marcellus Investment Managers, says India is an outlier. “No other large market charges capital gain tax to foreigners,” he told Business Standard. He says India does not follow the usual practice of leaving foreign investors to be taxed in their home country. Mukherjea says the 12.5 per cent headline rate understates the burden. By his account, adding STT, surcharge and GST brings the effective rate to about 15 per cent, and the cash that foreign funds set aside for future tax takes the overall tax cost to 16-16.5 per cent. He says the MSCI India index, which foreign funds use as a benchmark for Indian equities, has returned as little as 7 per cent over 10 years in dollar terms after netting off taxes. He says the issue did not matter before 2018, when long-term gains were not taxed, and that foreign selling picked up after the 2024 increase. He puts the outflow at about $70 billion over two years and describes artificial intelligence (AI)-related swings as transient, with tax as a structural factor. The case for a targeted approach Akhil Chandna, partner and global people solutions leader at Grant Thornton Bharat, does not back a blanket exemption, meaning no capital gains tax at all for foreign investors. “I am not saying abolishing capital gains tax across the board,” he says in his written note. He suggests India could examine whether genuine long-term institutional FPIs should get an exemption or a concessional rate, while short-term speculative gains stay taxed, subject to holding-period and anti-abuse conditions. He also recommends, as a pre-Budget suggestion, that the government review and rationalise the framework so that it is more competitive for foreign investors. A full exemption for foreign investors, he adds, raises questions of tax neutrality when domestic investors continue to pay. Chandna also says India’s rates on its own residents are lower than those in several developed economies, though higher than in Singapore, Hong Kong and the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Pre-Budget consultations are on, and Agrawal said the outcome would be known on February 1. Whether any relief is limited to foreign investors or also covers Indian investors will be visible then.
